In general, the state is both willing and able to offer sufficient protection to persons fearing non-state, including ‘rogue’ state, actors. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.
Ethiopia has a constitution and other laws that protect fundamental human rights and penalise criminal activity. There is a functioning police force and judiciary, which are generally accessible.
However, the availability and effectiveness of protection may vary depending on the person’s profile, location and other circumstances. In areas affected by armed conflict, post-conflict insecurity, weak state presence or contested territorial control, the availability and effectiveness of protection may be reduced. It may also be difficult to access protection in rural areas. Availability and effectiveness of protection may also be reduced for perceived critics of the government, including political opponents, activists and journalists. Protection may be difficult to access for women.
See the relevant Ethiopia Country Policy and Information Notes for specific guidance and information on the willingness of the state to protect those of Amhara, Oromo or Tigrayan ethnicity and actual or perceived members and supporters of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) and Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Fano and Amhara political opposition groups and the Tigray Peoples Liberation Front (TPLF).
Each case must be considered on its individual facts. The onus is on the person to demonstrate that they are not able to obtain sufficient protection from the state.
This section considers relevant evidence – including country information , refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:
the state (or quasi-state bodies) can provide effective protection.
Each case must be considered on its individual facts.
For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes .
1. Material facts, credibility and other checks
assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status ).
check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants ).
consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process) ).
consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis ).

3.1.1 In general, the state is both willing and able to offer sufficient protection to persons fearing non-state, including ‘rogue’ state, actors. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.
3.1.2 Ethiopia has a constitution and other laws that protect fundamental human rights and penalise criminal activity. There is a functioning police force and judiciary, which are generally accessible. However, the availability and effectiveness of protection may vary depending on the person’s profile, location and other circumstances. In areas affected by armed conflict, post-conflict insecurity, weak state presence or contested territorial control, the availability and effectiveness of protection may be reduced. It may also be difficult to access protection in rural areas. Availability and effectiveness of protection may also be reduced for perceived critics of the government, including political opponents, activists and journalists. Protection may be difficult to access for women.
3.1.3 Although Ethiopia maintains a monopoly on the use of force in principle, armed groups continue to challenge state authority and exercise control or influence, including through control of territory. In parts of Amhara and Oromia, Fano and the OLA reportedly exercise control. Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) data indicate that non-state armed actors accounted for 57.8% of all violent incidents and 64.0% of the fatalities between 1 January 2024 and 9 October 2026. They also accounted for 64.9% of civilian targeting incidents and 54.8% of associated fatalities. ACLED defines civilian targeting as events in which civilians are the only or primary target of attack. Their continuing activity, particularly in areas where armed groups challenge state control, may also suggest reduced practical capacity of law-enforcement institutions to provide protection (see Non-state armed actors ).
3.1.4 Decision makers should also consult the relevant Ethiopia Country Policy and Information Notes for specific guidance and information on the willingness of the state to protect those of Amhara, Oromo or Tigrayan ethnicity and actual or perceived members and supporters of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) and Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Fano and Amhara political opposition groups and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
3.1.5 Ethiopian security forces, both national and regional, are implicated in violence against civilians and other human rights violations. ACLED data shows that state actors—the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), federal police and state police—were responsible for 35% of reported civilian-targeting incidents and 45.2% of the associated fatalities. State actors also contributed to 42.2% of all violent events and 36% of associated fatalities (see Violence against civilians and ACLED data on forced disappearances/abductions ).
3.1.6 Ethiopia has a legal and institutional framework to protect human rights and investigate, prosecute and punish criminal acts constituting persecution or serious harm. The Constitution provides for equality before the law, personal liberty and security, and protection from torture and other forms of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Criminal Code criminalises a range of offences, including unlawful arrest and detention. Ethiopia has ratified several key international and regional human rights instruments (see Legal Framework ). However, corruption, resource constraints, insecurity, limited judicial independence and alleged human rights abuses by some state actors hamper the effectiveness of protection in practice but does not mean that protection is generally unavailable. Women seeking protection may face inaccessible facilities, language barriers, limited police understanding of gender-based violence, victim-blaming, inadequate shelter and rehabilitation services, and customary justice mechanisms in which women are underrepresented, and gender equality is not consistently upheld. These barriers are likely to be greater in rural, remote and conflict-affected areas and where the alleged perpetrator is connected to the authorities or local power structures (see Human rights violations by security forces , Rule of law and judiciary , Law enforcement and institutions and Courts ).
3.1.7 Ethiopia has constitutionally defined federal and regional security and law enforcement structures, including the federal and regional police commissions, federal and regional police forces, the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and intelligence services. The Federal Police Commission is responsible for investigating federal crimes, executing court orders, maintaining public order in specified circumstances and supporting regional law enforcement where authorised, while regional police have responsibility for local crime and immediate response within their jurisdictions. The ENDF may provide internal security support in some circumstances. Prosecution of federal cases falls primarily to the Ministry of Justice, while State Justice Bureaus have similar functions at regional level (see Prosecution and investigation and Security forces ).
3.1.8 Reliable and comprehensive national crime statistics are not publicly available, partly because Ethiopia lacks a national criminal information database. Nevertheless, available sources indicate that crime and insecurity remain significant concerns in parts of the country. Reported criminal activity includes robbery, assault, banditry, cattle raiding, kidnapping for ransom, human trafficking and migrant smuggling, with higher levels of insecurity reported in conflict-affected areas of Amhara, Oromia and Tigray. Survey data also suggests that concerns about personal safety are widespread, with a significant proportion of respondents reporting feeling unsafe in their neighbourhoods or fearing crime in their homes. Data on violence against civilians indicates that both state and non-state actors continued to be responsible for a substantial number of incidents and fatalities during the reporting period. While the available data points to a decline in recorded civilian-targeting incidents and fatalities between 2024 and 9 October 2026, violence remained at a significant level and varied considerably between regions (see Levels of crime and violence ).
3.1.9 Ethiopia has a functioning law-enforcement system with trained personnel and specialised structures for addressing particular forms of criminality, including human trafficking and organised crime. However, challenges in identifying victims and protecting victims and witnesses, as well as corruption and official complicity in human trafficking crimes, affect the prosecution of trafficking cases. The authorities have taken steps to strengthen institutional capacity through human rights and professional training for police, prosecutors, judges, security personnel and prison staff. Sources indicate that law-enforcement agencies can investigate and prosecute criminal offences in some circumstances, although much of the available reporting on institutional capacity consists of statements by government officials rather than independent assessments (see Security forces and Capacity and effectiveness of law enforcement agencies ).
3.1.10 Survey data indicates mixed public perceptions of the police, with many respondents able to access assistance when needed but fewer considering police officers to act professionally and with respect for citizens’ rights. Allegations of excessive use of force, particularly during arrests and public demonstrations, also indicate ongoing concerns regarding police conduct. The overall effectiveness of law enforcement is further affected by insecurity in conflict-affected areas, the presence of non-state armed groups, corruption, resource constraints and weaknesses in the rule of law. Consequently, the ability of the authorities to provide effective policing and protection is likely to vary depending on the location and the prevailing security situation (see Capacity and effectiveness of law enforcement agencies and Non-state actors ).
3.1.11 Corruption is widespread and affects the effectiveness of state protection, but it does not prevent the functioning of the criminal justice system. The government has established a legal and institutional framework to combat corruption and has taken enforcement action against public officials. However, sources consistently report that corruption persists within law enforcement, public administration and the judiciary. Bribery involving police officers and court officials has been reported, and perceptions of corruption within these institutions remain relatively high. Survey data indicates that 35% of those who sought police assistance had to pay a bribe, give a gift or do a favour to obtain it. Government anti-corruption measures have had some effect but have not eliminated systemic corruption (see Corruption ).
3.1.12 Although Ethiopia’s constitution and legal framework provide for an independent judiciary, and recent reforms have sought to strengthen judicial autonomy, judicial independence remains limited in practice. The judiciary continues to face political influence over appointments and decision-making, executive interference, corruption, and pressure on judges and prosecutors. There are also concerns that the courts have contributed to impunity for members of the security forces, particularly in cases involving political detainees. Between December 2024 and February 2025, judges in the Amhara region were reportedly arrested in connection with judicial decisions, while other judicial officials reportedly resigned due to threats, insecurity, and inadequate protection. The effectiveness of the justice system is further undermined by shortages of judicial personnel, limited training and resources, delays in case processing, and difficulties in enforcing some court rulings (see Judicial independence ).
3.1.13 Ethiopia has a functioning and multi-layered judicial system comprising federal and regional courts, as well as Sharia courts, customary courts and Community Justice Centres. Customary and community-based mechanisms play an important role in dispute resolution, particularly in rural areas and in regions where indigenous justice systems are widely recognised and used. These mechanisms appear to increase access to justice for some individuals and resolve a significant proportion of disputes. However, demand for justice continues to exceed the capacity of existing institutions, with around 5 million of an estimated 7 million legal problems arising annually remaining unresolved. The high volume of cases handled by prosecutors and the reported conviction rate suggest that the formal criminal justice system remains operational. Nevertheless, case backlogs, resource constraints and concerns regarding the operation of some customary justice mechanisms indicate that access to effective remedies and timely justice is uneven across regions and types of disputes. Access to justice is further limited for certain groups, including persons with disabilities and non-Amharic speakers (see Courts , Access ).
3.1.4 Ethiopia’s legal framework provides safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention and guarantees due process and fair trial rights, including judicial oversight of detention, access to legal representation, the presumption of innocence and the right of appeal. However, these protections are not consistently upheld in practice. Reported concerns include arbitrary detention, delays in bringing detainees before a court, non-compliance with some court orders, and limited access to legal safeguards from the outset of detention. Questions have also been raised regarding respect for due process and fair trial standards, particularly in cases involving government critics and other politically sensitive matters. The Committee against Torture stated that torture was routinely used to obtain confessions and that such confessions had been admitted as evidence in criminal proceedings. In addition, shortages of judicial personnel and resources contribute to delays in case processing and undermine the timely administration of justice (see Rule of law and Fair trial ).
3.1.15 Legal aid services are available through a range of government institutions, statutory bodies, universities, professional associations and civil society organisations. In 2023 Ethiopia adopted a National Free Legal Aid Strategy to improve the coordination, quality and accessibility of legal assistance, particularly for vulnerable groups. The number of individuals reported to have received legal aid through federal and regional institutions indicates that such services are operating in practice. Nevertheless, legal aid provision remains constrained by limited resources and uneven geographical coverage, with access reportedly more restricted in some rural and remote areas. The Human Rights Committee noted that legal aid is currently mandatory only for persons accused of serious crimes (see Legal aid ).
3.1.16 Ethiopia has a comprehensive legal and institutional framework for witness protection, including safeguards against intimidation and retaliation, a broad range of protective and support measures, and a dedicated directorate within the Ministry of Justice to assess applications and oversee protection. These provisions apply principally to serious crimes and are reinforced by specific legislation covering terrorism, corruption, trafficking and smuggling. Protection measures are used in practice, including victim support, video testimony and child-friendly interview facilities. However, the Ministry of Justice has reported that the witness protection proclamation currently in force contains fundamental legal gaps and problems with its implementation. Ethiopia scored 3.00 out of 10 on victim and witness support, non-state actors remain the primary providers of support for survivors of conflict-related sexual violence, and protection services reportedly remained limited, with concerns about reprisals discouraging some victims from participating in criminal proceedings (see Witness protection ).
3.1.17 Ethiopia retains the death penalty and has not established an official moratorium, although no executions have been carried out since 2007. About 130 people were under sentence of death as of April 2025, with more than 5 death sentences imposed during 2025. The death penalty remains available for offences that do not involve intentional killing, including under counter-terrorism legislation for acts causing serious damage to property, historical or cultural heritage or the natural environment. Ethiopia has not joined the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR and its position on abolition is unchanged ( Death penalty ).
3.1.18 Detention conditions in Ethiopia are generally poor and are characterised by overcrowding and inadequate living conditions. Despite measures aimed at improving prison infrastructure and detainee welfare, concerns remain regarding sanitation, healthcare, food provision and accommodation in some facilities. There are also allegations of torture and ill-treatment, alongside concerns about unofficial detention sites and limited safeguards for vulnerable detainees. However, conditions appear to vary between prisons and detention centres, and recent government initiatives suggest some efforts to address longstanding deficiencies (see Prison capacity and Detention conditions ).
3.1.19 Ethiopia has a legal framework that prohibits torture, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrest and detention, and enforced disappearance, and provides safeguards intended to protect fundamental rights. However, state and non-state actors reportedly engage in torture and ill-treatment, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary and prolonged detention, and enforced disappearances. These violations occur more frequently in conflict-affected areas and against persons perceived as opposing the government, including political opponents, journalists, human rights defenders, activists, academics, real or suspected supporters of armed groups, and members of certain ethnic groups. Legal safeguards are not consistently respected in practice and accountability for violations remains limited. Legislation passed in June 2025 grants undercover agents advance immunity for crimes committed during operations (see Torture and ill-treatment and Extrajudicial killings and excessive use of force and Arbitrary arrest and detention ).
3.1.20 Ethiopian law prohibits enforced disappearance and provides legal protections for liberty and personal security. However, sources report that state actors, including the police, intelligence services and the military engage in enforced disappearances particularly of individuals perceived as government critics, political opponents, journalists, activists and members of certain ethnic groups, specifically Amhara and Oromos. At the same time, available data indicates that non-state armed actors also engage in abductions and forced disappearances. ACLED recorded 262 abduction/forced disappearance events from January 2024 to July 2026, involving at least 2,033 people. OLA was responsible for 22.9% of the events, Fano for 21.0% and government security forces for 11.1% of the events (see Enforced disappearance ).
3.1.21 Ethiopia adopted a Transitional Justice Policy in April 2024 to support accountability, truth-seeking, reconciliation and reparations for violations committed during conflict. However, implementation has been slow and, despite some investigations, prosecutions and convictions, impunity for serious human rights violations remains widespread and accountability is limited relative to the scale of reported abuses (see Accountability for violations committed during conflict ).
3.1.22 Ethiopia has formal mechanisms for the oversight of public administration and human rights, including the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) and the Office of the Ombudsman. These institutions investigate allegations of maladministration and human rights violations and provide avenues for complaints and redress. However, sources reported limitations in the effectiveness of these oversight mechanisms. Complaint procedures available to detainees were described as lacking independence and effectiveness, and complainants were reported to face intimidation or reprisals. Sources also indicated that independent monitoring of places of detention is limited, with the EHRC not always granted unrestricted access to detention facilities. In addition, resource constraints, the absence of a National Preventive Mechanism to monitor places of detention, and concerns regarding the EHRC’s operational independence were identified as factors affecting the ability of oversight bodies to provide effective scrutiny and accountability (see Oversight mechanisms ).
3.1.23 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status .
The COI provides the basis for the assessment and the executive summary. Decision makers must use relevant COI as the evidential basis for decisions.
The cut-off date for COI included in this note is 15 October 2026.
